title: Systemic disease
description: Oral and dental manifestations of systemic disease — the moment when a routine dental exam picks up an undiagnosed haematological, endocrine, autoimmune, or metabolic condition.

problems.description: Gums swell and bleed spontaneously, with petechial spots on the palate and mucosal pallor; candidosis or herpetic ulcers arise without obvious local cause.
problems.etiology: Acute leukaemia causes a neoplastic proliferation of white blood cells, releasing primitive blast cells into the peripheral blood [2]. Marrow infiltration reduces resistance to infection and impairs haemostasis, producing the oral signs [1]. Acute myeloid leukaemia is the commonest acute leukaemia of adults; acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the commonest childhood leukaemia [2].
problems.presentation: Gingival swelling and hypertrophy are characteristic [1]. Spontaneous gingival bleeding occurs even with minimal trauma, alongside petechial haemorrhages on the palate and buccal mucosa [1]. Mucosal pallor reflects the underlying anaemia. Oral candidosis and herpetic infections arise because resistance to infection is reduced [1]. The dental presentation can be the first sign of haematological malignancy, preceding systemic diagnosis.
problems.results: Blood picture will show abnormal white cell differential. Platelet count is low, explaining the haemorrhagic tendency. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may be controlled by using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing while awaiting haematological management [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of spontaneous gingival bleeding, gingival swelling, mucosal pallor, and opportunistic oral infections — occurring together, without a local periodontal explanation — is the defining cluster. Petechial haemorrhages on the palate with minimal or no trauma are particularly significant [1].
problems.treatment: The GDP's role is recognition and urgent same-day medical referral. Local measures to control bleeding include improving oral hygiene, avoiding extractions, and using local haemostatic methods [3]. Chlorhexidine mouthwashes help prevent superinfection; infections that arise must be treated aggressively [3]. All surgical intervention is deferred until haematological management is established. Liaise urgently with a haematologist.
problems.prognosis: Depends entirely on leukaemia type and stage at diagnosis. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children carries up to 90% cure rate in favourable cases; acute myeloid leukaemia in adults has high remission rates but a tendency to relapse [2]. Early detection — including via oral signs — improves outcome.

citations.quote: This and other haematological malignancies are associated with a ↓ in resistance to infection leading to candidosis or herpetic infections. Other oral problems include bleeding and petechial haemorrhage (even with minimal trauma), gingival swelling, ulceration, and mucosal pallor.

A neoplastic proliferation of white blood cells. Acute leukaemias are characterized by the release of primitive blast cells into the peripheral blood and account for 50% of childhood malignancy. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the commonest childhood leukaemia, now has up to 90% cure rate in favourable cases. May present as gingival hypertrophy and bleeding. Acute myeloid leukaemia is the commonest acute leukaemia of adults, with high remission rates possible but a tendency to relapse.

Prevention of superinfection with chlorhexidine mouthwashes and aggressive appropriate Rx of infections which arise are of real help. Management of the bleeding is aimed at the underlying disorder; local techniques include improving OH, avoiding extractions, and using local haemostatic methods. Spontaneous gingival bleeding may be controlled by using impressions as a made-to-measure pressure dressing.

In haematological malignancy, anaemia, bleeding, and infection are the overwhelming risks. Look for and treat anaemia. Avoid aspirin, other NSAIDs, trauma, and IM injections. Prevent sepsis, and if it occurs, treat very aggressively with the locally recommended broad-spectrum antibacterials and antifungals.

problems.description: Sore, atrophic tongue, angular cheilitis, and recurrent mouth ulcers in a patient with no obvious local cause; burning mouth without mucosal change may be the presenting sign.
problems.conditionName: Iron, B12, or folate deficiency — oral manifestations
problems.etiology: Iron, vitamin B12, and folate deficiency each impair mucosal integrity and epithelial turnover [1]. Deficiencies may be present before a frank anaemia is established biochemically — the oral signs can appear first [1]. Iron deficiency is most often due to chronic blood loss or inadequate diet; B12 deficiency arises in pernicious anaemia, alcohol abuse, small gut disease, or chronic nitrous oxide exposure; low folate is usually dietary [4].
problems.presentation: Atrophic glossitis — formerly the commonest oral symptom of anaemia — produces a smooth, sore tongue [1]. Red lines or patches on a sore but otherwise normal-looking tongue may indicate B12 deficiency [1]. Recurrent aphthous ulceration is associated with all three deficiencies [1]. Angular cheilitis is a well-recognised association with iron deficiency and general anaemia [3]. The sore, clinically normal tongue (burning tongue) is sometimes a manifestation or even precursor of anaemia [1]. Candidosis may be precipitated or exacerbated by anaemia, particularly iron deficiency [1].
problems.results: Full blood count may show microcytic hypochromic picture in iron deficiency or macrocytosis in B12/folate deficiency. Serum iron, B12, and folate levels confirm the deficiency [2]. Clinical features of anaemia — pallor of conjunctivae and palmar creases, brittle or spoon-shaped nails — may accompany the oral signs [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Oral signs preceding or coinciding with haematinic deficiency, in the absence of local mucosal disease. The triad of sore atrophic tongue, angular cheilitis, and recurrent aphthae — especially in a young or middle-aged woman — is the classic cluster. Burning mouth without mucosal change as a precursor of anaemia is a less recognised but documented feature [1].
problems.treatment: The GDP's role is recognition, haematinic screening (FBC, B12, folate, serum iron/ferritin), and referral to the GP or haematologist for cause investigation and correction [2]. Local topical treatment of oral lesions provides symptom relief but does not address the underlying deficiency. Correction of the deficiency resolves oral signs. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg three times daily for iron; lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg 3-monthly for B12 deficiency; folic acid 5 mg daily for folate deficiency — these are prescribed by the physician [2].
problems.prognosis: Oral signs resolve with correction of the underlying deficiency. Pernicious anaemia requires lifelong B12 replacement. Recurrence of oral signs after treatment is a prompt to recheck haematinics.

citations.quote: The nutritional deficiencies associated with anaemia, iron, vitamin B12, and folate, are all associated with recurrent oral ulceration and specific deficiencies may be present, even in the absence of a frank anaemia. Atrophic glossitis was formerly the commonest oral symptom of anaemia but is less often seen now. Red lines or patches on a sore, but normal-looking tongue may indicate vitamin B12 deficiency. Candidosis may be precipitated or exacerbated by anaemia, particularly iron deficiency, and angular cheilitis is a well-recognized association. The sore, clinically normal tongue (burning tongue) is sometimes a manifestation or even precursor of anaemia.

In all cases the cause must be sought; this may necessitate referral to a haematologist. Drugs used in iron deficiency: ferrous sulfate 200mg tds. Lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin 1mg 3-monthly is used to treat vitamin B12 deficiency, and folic acid 5mg od for folate deficiency.

These are notoriously unreliable, but may include general fatigue, heart failure, angina on effort, pallor (look at conjunctivae and palmar creases, but unreliable), brittle nails &/or spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), oral discomfort &/or ulceration, glossitis, and classically angular cheilitis.

Vitamin B12 is ↓ in pernicious anaemia (deficit of intrinsic factor), alcohol abuse, small gut disease, and chronic exposure to nitrous oxide. Low folate is usually dietary, but may be caused by illness (e.g. coeliac disease, skin disease) or drugs such as phenytoin, methotrexate, trimethoprim, and co-trimoxazole.

problems.description: Severe or rapidly progressive periodontal disease, dry mouth, and oral thrush in a patient whose glycaemic control is poor; burning mouth or slow healing after extractions may accompany these signs.
problems.etiology: Persistent hyperglycaemia impairs leucocyte function and tissue perfusion, reducing resistance to infection [1]. In poorly controlled diabetes, this reduced resistance drives severe periodontal disease and oral candidosis [1]. Xerostomia and thrush are prominent features of ketoacidosis specifically [1]. Peripheral neuropathy in established diabetes can present as oral or facial dysaesthesia or burning mouth [1]. Sialosis is a late feature [1].
problems.presentation: Severe periodontal disease disproportionate to the patient's plaque control is the most important oral sign [1]. Xerostomia compounds this by reducing salivary protection [1]. Oral candidiasis, including angular cheilitis, arises from the impaired immune response [1]. Burning mouth or facial dysaesthesia may reflect peripheral neuropathy [1]. Slower-than-expected healing after extractions or oral surgery is a consistent feature [1]. Lichenoid reactions on the buccal mucosa may follow from oral hypoglycaemic drugs [1].
problems.results: No specific oral lesion is pathognomonic, but the clustering of accelerated periodontal breakdown, dry mouth, recurrent candidiasis, and slow surgical healing — especially without a local explanation — prompts screening. Fasting blood glucose or HbA1c confirms the diagnosis. Management of the diabetic patient undergoing surgery requires specific planning around glycaemic control.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Accelerated periodontal disease in a patient with seemingly adequate plaque control, especially combined with xerostomia and recurrent candidiasis. The bilateral parotid swelling of sialosis, when present as a late finding, is a visible marker. Oral burning or dysaesthesia without mucosal cause in an older patient raises peripheral neuropathy from diabetes as a differential.
problems.treatment: The GDP's role is recognition and referral to the GP for glycaemic screening. Periodontal treatment follows standard protocols but should be coordinated with medical management — periodontal inflammation itself worsens glycaemic control bidirectionally. Oral surgery requires specific planning; there is a tendency to slower healing following surgery [1]. Lichenoid drug reactions should prompt discussion with the prescribing physician about alternative hypoglycaemics [1].
problems.prognosis: Oral complications are proportional to glycaemic control. Improved control reduces susceptibility to periodontal breakdown, candidosis, and delayed healing. Peripheral neuropathic oral symptoms may be less reversible once established.

citations.quote: No specific oral changes, although manifestations of ↓ resistance to infection can be seen if poorly controlled (e.g. severe periodontal disease). Xerostomia and thrush are prominent features of ketoacidosis. Sialosis is sometimes seen as a late feature of diabetes. Burning mouth may be a presenting feature, and oral or facial dysaesthesia may reflect the peripheral neuropathies seen in diabetics. There is a tendency to slower healing following surgery. Lichenoid reactions due to oral hypoglycaemic drugs may be seen.
Persistent hyperglycaemia due to a relative deficiency of insulin.

problems.description: Loss of lamina dura on dental radiographs, ground-glass bone pattern in the jaws, or a multilocular cystic jaw lesion found incidentally on routine radiography.
problems.conditionName: Hyperparathyroidism — jaw lesions and lamina dura loss
problems.etiology: Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by hyperplasia or adenoma of the parathyroid glands [1]. Raised parathormone mobilises calcium from bone, causing generalised bone demineralisation [1]. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a response to low plasma calcium, for example in renal failure; tertiary follows when parathyroid overproduction persists even after calcium is normalised [2]. Irreversible renal damage occurs in the absence of treatment, so early detection matters [1].
problems.presentation: In the jaws, the radiographic findings are the key dental presentation: loss of the lamina dura around teeth, a generalised 'ground-glass' trabecular pattern replacing the normal bone architecture, and cystic radiolucent lesions that often appear multilocular [1]. These cysts contain dark-coloured tissue and are histologically identical to giant cell granuloma — the 'brown tumour' [1]. The jaw radiograph is often where the condition is first identified, ahead of any systemic symptoms.
problems.results: Biochemistry confirms raised serum calcium, raised PTH, and lowered alkaline phosphatase [1]. The diagnosis is confirmed by the combination of raised Ca²⁺ and raised PTH [1]. The brown tumour histologically shows multinucleate giant cells indistinguishable from giant cell granuloma on biopsy alone — systemic biochemistry is required to distinguish the two [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Loss of lamina dura is not specific to hyperparathyroidism but its combination with ground-glass jaw bone and a multilocular giant-cell lesion — particularly in a patient with unexplained renal impairment — defines the radiographic triad. Bilateral or multi-site brown tumours are strongly suggestive. The condition is rare but worth detecting because of the risk of irreversible renal damage if left untreated [1].
problems.treatment: The GDP's role is recognition on routine radiography and urgent medical referral. Any jaw lesion fitting this radiographic pattern — especially in the absence of prior local explanation — warrants blood calcium and PTH measurement. Surgical treatment of the parathyroid lesion (adenoma excision or subtotal parathyroidectomy) is the physician's domain. Brown tumours in the jaw typically regress after successful parathyroid surgery and do not require independent jaw surgery in most cases.
problems.prognosis: Prognosis with early treatment is good. The major risk of delayed diagnosis is irreversible renal damage [1]. Brown tumours regress following correction of hyperparathyroidism. Recurrence depends on whether the parathyroid pathology is fully excised.

citations.quote: Rare. Caused by hyperplasia or adenoma of the parathyroids. ↑ parathormone causes ↑ plasma Ca2+ liberated from bone. Irreversible renal damage in absence of Rx so worth detecting (diagnosis confirmed by ↑ Ca2+, ↑ PTH, ↓ alkaline phosphatase). Appears in the jaws as loss of lamina dura; a 'ground-glass' appearance of bone and cystic lesions (often looking multilocular), which contain dark-coloured tissue; 'brown tumour' histologically indistinguishable from a giant cell granuloma.
1° is caused by an adenoma. 2° is a response to low plasma Ca2+, e.g. in renal failure, and 3° follows on from 2° when the parathyroids continue ↑ production, even if Ca2+ is normalized.

problems.description: Persistent linear oral ulcers, cobblestoning of the buccal mucosa with mucosal tags, or diffuse lip swelling without obvious local cause; oral features may predate gut symptoms.
problems.etiology: Crohn's disease is a chronic granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology affecting any part of the gut from mouth to anus [1]. Approximately 1% of cases present with oral ulceration predating any other symptoms [1]. Orofacial granulomatosis is probably a variant of the same process, and may represent a hypersensitivity response to certain foods or additives such as benzoates [2].
problems.presentation: Oral lesions affect the gingiva, buccal mucosa, and lips [1]. The characteristic features are purplish-red non-haemorrhagic swellings, linear long-standing ulcers, cobblestoning of the buccal mucosa, and mucosal tags and folds [1]. Lip swelling (granulomatous cheilitis) is a visible and sometimes striking sign. These lesions may appear years before gastrointestinal symptoms, placing the GDP in the position of first detection [1].
problems.results: Biopsy of oral tissue demonstrating non-caseating granulomata is the key histological finding [2]. Gastrointestinal investigations and imaging are required to establish the extent of gut involvement. Haematinic deficiency and anaemia may coexist from malabsorption.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Linear, persistent, non-healing oral ulcers combined with cobblestone mucosal texture and mucosal tags are the hallmark oral presentation. The association with lip swelling (orofacial granulomatosis pattern) further strengthens clinical suspicion. These features are distinct from common aphthous ulceration in their linearity, persistence, and the cobblestone pattern of adjacent mucosa [1].
problems.treatment: The GDP's role is recognition and referral to gastroenterology or general medicine. Painful oral lesions respond well to topical steroids or simple excision, but treatment is ultimately aimed at the systemic disease [1]. For orofacial granulomatosis, identification and avoidance of irritant dietary factors — particularly benzoates — is the most beneficial approach [2]. Severe cases may require systemic therapy with sulfasalazine or infliximab [2]. The GDP should not manage these lesions in isolation without medical coordination.
problems.prognosis: Oral manifestations tend to parallel the activity of the systemic disease. Successful management of intestinal Crohn's often improves oral lesions. Some oral signs may persist independently. Orofacial granulomatosis without confirmed gut disease can sometimes be controlled by dietary modification alone [2].

citations.quote: Chronic granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology affecting any part of the gut from mouth to anus. Primarily affects the terminal third of the ileum, although ~1% of cases will present with oral ulceration predating any other symptoms. These tend to affect the gingiva, buccal mucosa, and lips with purplish-red non-haemorrhagic swellings, linear long-standing ulcers and cobblestoning of buccal mucosa with mucosal tags and folds. Orofacial granulomatosis is probably a variant. Painful oral lesions seem to respond well to topical steroids or simple excision but Rx is aimed at the systemic disease.

This is clinically and histologically identical to oral manifestations of Crohn's disease. ∆ of exclusion (Crohn's, sarcoid). Probable aetiology is as a hypersensitivity response to certain foods, additives such as benzoates, etc. ∆ is biopsy to demonstrate granulomata histologically and exclusion of systemic disease. Most beneficial Rx is to identify and avoid the irritant factors. Patients who have generalized Crohn's or very severe orofacial granulomatosis may benefit from systemic Rx with sulfasalazine or infliximab.

Crohn's disease may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract but has a preference for the ileo-caecal area. It is a chronic granulomatous disease affecting the full thickness of the mucosa and may result in fistula formation.

problems.description: Wound oozing restarts an hour or more after extraction, continuing as a slow intractable bleed after the initial clot appeared to form normally.
problems.etiology: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII, affecting males predominantly, although female haemophiliacs can occur [1]. All daughters of affected males are potential carriers [1]. Severity of bleeding is dependent on the level of factor VIII activity and the degree of trauma [1]. Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease) is clinically identical [2].
problems.presentation: Bleeding from the mouth is common in haemophilia [1]. The characteristic pattern is that following trauma, bleeding appears to stop initially as the platelet plug forms, but an intractable general ooze starts after an hour or so [1]. This delayed-onset ooze — not immediate gushing — is the defining clinical behaviour. Haemarthroses are the more common systemic presentation, typically appearing in childhood [1].
problems.results: Prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelet count is the screening profile. Factor VIII assay confirms the diagnosis and quantifies severity. Most patients with haemophilia A will have disclosed the condition on their medical history; the presenting sign at a GDP is more likely to be unexplained prolonged post-extraction ooze in an undiagnosed or unrecognised case [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The one-hour delay before ooze restarts is the pathognomonic behavioural pattern — it distinguishes factor deficiency from platelet disorders, where bleeding is immediate. The absence of obvious local cause for the prolonged bleed, combined with a history of easy bruising or haemarthroses, directs the diagnosis [1].
problems.treatment: The haemophilias should always be managed at specialist centres; the GDP should check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number [3]. Factor cover before any surgical intervention is mandatory and is arranged with the specialist haemophilia centre. No surgical procedure — including extractions — should be undertaken in the primary care setting without prior specialist liaison and factor replacement cover. Local haemostatic measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion are adjuncts for established bleeding but do not replace factor correction [4].
problems.prognosis: With appropriate factor replacement cover, dental and oral surgical procedures can be completed safely. Unplanned extraction without cover carries a serious risk of life-threatening haemorrhage. Advances in recombinant factor concentrates and prophylactic regimens have greatly improved the long-term outlook for haemophilia A.

citations.quote: The commonest clotting defect. Inherited as a sex-linked recessive, it affects males predominantly, although female haemophiliacs can occur. All daughters of affected males are potential carriers. Usually presents in childhood as haemarthroses. Bleeding from the mouth is common. Following trauma, bleeding appears to stop, but an intractable general ooze starts after an hour or so. Severity of bleeding is dependent on the level of factor VIII activity and degree of trauma.
Clinically identical to haemophilia A; also known as Christmas disease.
The haemophilias and Von Willebrand's disease should always be managed at specialist centres. Check the patient's warning card for the contact telephone number.
If actively bleeding, use a combination of local measures, tranexamic acid, and platelet transfusion.
